I am looking to do a week long hike this year on the Applachian Trail but was thinking that an off trail hike might be more fun. I am in the SE and do not know if any good places.

Do people just check into a national forest with a gps or compass / map and go for it or what? I want to spend a few days out in nature and the AT is getting too crowded lately. Bumping in to other people all day is not the experience that I am looking for.
Anyone do any wilderness hiking before?

You may want to look into the Linville Gorge just south of Boone, NC. There are numerous trails that take you from the top of the mountain down to the river below. Spend some time hiking into the depths of it and I doubt you would encounter many people. The whole gorge is a primitive national party but the good news is that the surrounding area is pretty populous so you don't have to worry about being lost for days on end without running into some form of help.

Decades ago we used to go for day-long hikes where we took our breakfast and lunch with us, but I am the kind of hiker where I still want a hot shower and soft bed at the end of the day.

When I go on off trail hikes I have always looked at maps and planned possible routes in advance. I suggest checking the USGS for 15 minute maps at the 1:24,000 scale. They provide a great deal of information about the type of terrain you are likely to encounter. I have done 4 off trail hikes and would love to share my experiences. AMA

This is happening to me as well, and while I know that this is not a support forum, I do think it had something to do with a driver issue.

It looks like you're using a 32-bit steam binary (or library) on a 64-bit Linux build. You may need to find a version of steam compiled specifically for 64-bit. Debian repositories may have the correct build, so you could try removing steam and installing from the repositories. There is a bit more information here regarding 64-bit builds.

The main thing to take away here is that unless you really know what you're doing, don't use bleeding edge Debian installs. Debian is slow to update, but that's why it's usually very stable.
